t: Group 16 Trends and Oxides of Sulfur
def: Group 16 (oxygen family) elements show increasing atomic size and metallic character down the group, and sulfur forms important oxides like sulfur dioxide and sulfur trioxide.
points: Group 16 order: O, S, Se, Te, Po; atomic and ionic radii increase down the group.
Electronegativity and non-metallic character decrease down the group; oxygen is most non-metallic.
Oxidation states shown: -2 common for all; +4 and +6 shown by S, Se, Te.
SO2 is prepared by burning sulfur in air or roasting sulfide ores; it is a colourless, pungent gas, used to make sulfuric acid.
SO3 is formed by catalytic oxidation of SO2 (2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3) in the Contact process.
SO2 has a V-shaped (angular) structure; SO3 has a planar trigonal structure in the gas phase.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Sulfur burnt in air"] --> B["SO2 formed"]
  B --> C["Catalytic oxidation with O2"]
  C --> D["SO3 formed"]
  D --> E["Dissolved in water gives H2SO4"]

example: Industrial Contact process: S burnt to SO2, then SO2 oxidised to SO3 over V2O5 catalyst at 720 K, then SO3 absorbed in water to give H2SO4.
tip: Write balanced equations for both SO2 formation and its conversion to SO3 — these reactions are commonly asked for 2 marks.

def: Oxoacids of sulfur are acids containing sulfur, oxygen and hydrogen, such as sulfurous acid and sulfuric acid, important in industry and the laboratory.
points: Sulfurous acid, H2SO3, is formed when SO2 dissolves in water; it is a weak diprotic acid.
Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, is a strong dibasic acid, manufactured by the Contact process.
In H2SO4, sulfur is tetrahedrally surrounded by two OH groups and two oxygen atoms (two S=O double bonds).
H2SO4 is used in fertiliser manufacture, in batteries, and as a dehydrating and oxidising agent.
Oleum (H2S2O7, pyrosulfuric acid) is formed when SO3 is absorbed in concentrated H2SO4; diluting oleum with water gives H2SO4 back.
formula: SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3     SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4

diagram.draw: Draw the sulfuric acid molecule: a central S atom. Draw two double bonds going up to two O atoms labelled '=O'. Draw two single bonds going down-left and down-right to two OH groups. Label the shape as tetrahedral around sulfur.

example: Dilution of oleum: H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4, done carefully by adding acid to water to control the large heat release.
tip: Draw the structure of H2SO4 clearly with S=O and S-OH bonds shown — structure questions carry easy marks.

t: Group 17 Trends and Preparation of Halogens
def: Group 17 (halogens) are highly reactive non-metals whose reactivity decreases down the group, and they are prepared industrially and in the laboratory by oxidation of halide ions.
points: Group 17 order: F, Cl, Br, I; all are diatomic, coloured, and strong oxidising agents.
Oxidising power and electronegativity decrease down the group (F2 is strongest oxidiser).
Chlorine is manufactured industrially by Deacon's process: oxidation of HCl gas with air using a CuCl2 catalyst.
Deacon's process reaction: 4HCl + O2 --(CuCl2, heat)--> 2Cl2 + 2H2O.
In the laboratory, Cl2 is made by heating MnO2 with concentrated HCl.
Bromine and iodine are obtained by oxidising Br- and I- ions in brine or seaweed extracts using Cl2 gas.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["HCl gas and air"] --> B["Pass over CuCl2 catalyst, heat"]
  B --> C["Chlorine gas produced"]
  C --> D["Water vapour byproduct"]

example: Laboratory preparation of chlorine: MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O, by gently heating the mixture.
tip: Name the catalyst (CuCl2) and the role of oxidation of chloride to chlorine clearly in Deacon's process answer.

def: Oxoacids of halogens are acids of chlorine (and other halogens) containing oxygen, whose acid strength increases as the oxidation state of the halogen increases.
points: Chlorine forms four main oxoacids: hypochlorous (HOCl), chlorous (HOClO), chloric (HOClO2), and perchloric (HOClO3) acid.
Oxidation state of Cl increases from +1 in HOCl to +7 in HClO4.
Acid strength increases in the order HOCl < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4, as more oxygen atoms stabilise the negative charge on the conjugate base.
Oxidising power decreases in the same order (HOCl is the strongest oxidiser, HClO4 the weakest among them).
All these acids are unstable and cannot usually be isolated pure; they exist mainly in aqueous solution or as salts.
formula: Acid strength: HOCl < HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["HOCl, Cl +1"] --> B["HClO2, Cl +3"]
  B --> C["HClO3, Cl +5"]
  C --> D["HClO4, Cl +7"]
  D --> E["Acid strength increases this way"]

example: Perchloric acid (HClO4) is the strongest oxoacid of chlorine because the +7 oxidation state gives the most stable, highly delocalised conjugate base ClO4-.
tip: Remember the trend as 'more oxygens, stronger acid, weaker oxidiser' — a quick way to answer ranking questions.

def: Interhalogen compounds are formed between two different halogen atoms, usually a larger halogen combined with one, three, five or seven smaller halogen atoms.
points: General formulas: AX, AX3, AX5, AX7, where A is the larger, less electronegative halogen and X is the smaller one.
They are formed by direct combination of halogens, e.g., Cl2 + F2 -> 2ClF.
AX type (like ClF, BrCl) is linear in shape.
AX3 type (like ClF3) has a bent T-shape; AX5 type (like ClF5) is square pyramidal; AX7 type (like IF7) is pentagonal bipyramidal.
Interhalogens are generally more reactive than the parent halogens (except fluorine) because the A-X bond is weaker than X-X bond.
They are used as fluorinating agents and oxidising agents in various reactions.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Two different halogens combine"] --> B["AX type: linear, e.g. ClF"]
  A --> C["AX3 type: bent T-shape, e.g. ClF3"]
  A --> D["AX5 type: square pyramidal, e.g. ClF5"]
  A --> E["AX7 type: pentagonal bipyramidal, e.g. IF7"]

example: IF7 is the largest known interhalogen; iodine (larger, less electronegative) is surrounded by seven fluorine atoms in a pentagonal bipyramidal shape.
tip: Learn one example and its correct shape for each formula type (AX, AX3, AX5, AX7) — shape-naming questions are common.

def: Noble gases (Group 18) have complete octets and are chemically mostly inert, but heavier noble gases, especially xenon, can form compounds with highly electronegative elements like fluorine and oxygen.
points: Noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn; they have full outer shells, giving very low reactivity.
Reactivity increases down the group as ionisation enthalpy decreases, making larger atoms (Kr, Xe) more reactive.
Xenon forms fluorides by direct reaction with fluorine under controlled conditions: Xe + F2 -> XeF2, Xe + 2F2 -> XeF4, Xe + 3F2 -> XeF6.
XeF2 is linear in shape, XeF4 is square planar, and XeF6 is distorted octahedral.
Xenon fluorides hydrolyse with water to give xenon oxides, e.g. XeF6 hydrolyses to give XeO3.
Noble gas compounds are strong oxidising and fluorinating agents.
formula: Xe + F2 --(Ni vessel, heat)--> XeF2     Xe + 2F2 -> XeF4     Xe + 3F2 -> XeF6

diagram.draw: Draw three separate xenon fluoride structures. XeF2: a straight line F-Xe-F (linear). XeF4: a square with Xe at the centre and F atoms at the four corners (square planar). XeF6: Xe at the centre with six F atoms around it in a slightly distorted octahedral arrangement. Label each shape below the drawing.

example: Varying the ratio of Xe to F2 and reaction conditions (temperature, pressure) controls which xenon fluoride (XeF2, XeF4 or XeF6) is the major product.
tip: State the exact mole ratio of Xe to F2 for each fluoride and its shape — this exact-ratio detail is often tested.
